row: | DOC-A.1-101 | **INVOKE statement — behavior when invoking a non-COBOL method**, §14.9.23.4 GR2 b) (and the GR7 e) execution of a non-COBOL method), required + documented | **A non-COBOL method is never invoked: COBOL.NET provides no way to designate one, so every INVOKE reaches a method written in COBOL or fails.** Every method an INVOKE can reach is declared in a COBOL class definition of the compilation group. A REPOSITORY class specifier whose externalized name is a .NET type (`CLASS SB AS "System.Text.StringBuilder"`) does not bind to that type: `INVOKE SB "NEW" …` is the compile-time error COBOLNET0823 (`OoBinder.OoBindInvoke`), and naming it in `USAGE OBJECT REFERENCE SB` is COBOLNET0813. The members every .NET object carries (`ToString`, `GetHashCode`, `Equals`, …) are not methods of a COBOL object: on a typed receiver `INVOKE T "ToString"` is the compile-time error COBOLNET0825 (§14.9.23.3 SR4 b)); on a universal object reference, or with the method-name held in a data item, the runtime dispatch `CobolObject.__CobolInvoke` searches only the COBOL-declared methods of the object's class hierarchy, finds none, and sets **EC-OO-METHOD** (fatal, §14.9.23.4 GR7 b)), so an unhandled occurrence terminates the run unit. GR7 e)'s implementor-defined execution of a non-COBOL method therefore never occurs. COBOL-2002, 2014 and 2023 (COBOL-85 has no INVOKE). How a REPOSITORY class specifier that names no definition of the compilation group is resolved is open under kb/Work PB1086. | — |

record.notes: §14.9.23.4 GR2 b) (cite.py OK §14.9.23.4 2)) leaves a non-COBOL method's INVOKE behaviour to the implementor; COBOL.NET's determination is that none can be designated. Row written to §7 as DOC-A.1-101 (kb/Work PB1534/PB1522 step 3). No test pins the .NET-member case specifically (OoSpineTests.Universal_UnknownMethod_EcOoMethod and InvokeUnknownMethod_0825 pin a COBOL-unknown name through the same arm), hence Pinned by —. Adjacent open edge: REPOSITORY class resolution without an external repository, kb/Work PB1086. Side finding: the COBOLNET0825 message cites §14.9.23.3 SR4d; the rule for an object-class-name receiver is SR4 b) (cite.py OK §14.9.23.3 4) b)).

row: | DOC-A.1-103 | **I-O status — action taken for a fatal exception condition**, §9.1.13.1 (with §14.6.13.1.3 3)), required + documented | The fatal I-O status values are every value beginning with **3, 4 or 7**, and every value beginning with **9** — COBOL.NET defines all its 9x values fatal (`ExceptionCatalog.IsFatalIoStatus`; the only one defined is '90', item 110). The action depends on whether checking is enabled for the EC-I-O condition the status corresponds to (§9.1.13.1): **Checking NOT enabled** (the default in every edition, and the only possibility at COBOL-85, which has no TURN directive): **the run unit CONTINUES.** The status is stored in the FILE STATUS item if there is one, any applicable USE AFTER ERROR/EXCEPTION declarative for the file or its open mode is executed, and control then passes to the end of the statement that produced the status. A NOT AT END or NOT INVALID KEY phrase on that statement is ignored. This holds even when the program has neither a FILE STATUS item nor a declarative: the run unit keeps running after, for example, an OPEN INPUT of a missing file ('35') and a later READ of that unopened file ('47'), and ends normally. **Checking enabled** (`>>TURN EC-I-O CHECKING ON`, EC-ALL, or a level-3 name, COBOL-2002 onward): **the run unit is TERMINATED ABNORMALLY** once any applicable declarative or exception-checking PERFORM WHEN has run and completed normally, or immediately when none applies (§14.6.13.1.3 5) and 7)). The message is `abnormal run-unit termination: <exception-name> (fatal): I-O status <nn> on <file>` and the process exit code is non-zero. A RESUME executed in that declarative prevents the termination (§14.9.33). The run unit also continues when the statement's own ON EXCEPTION phrase handled the status. The fatal status of a SORT or MERGE implicit input or output transfer follows that statement's own rules (§14.6.13.1.3 2), §3 SORT/MERGE bullet). Implemented in the generated `__IoCheckEc` (`EcEmitter.EmitIoCheckEc`); with checking off the generated `__IoCheck` has no termination arm. A host I/O failure inside a sequential READ or WRITE does not yet produce status '30' and is handled by neither arm (kb/Work PB1512). | `conformance-test:ExceptionConditionConformanceTests.IoPermanentError_Enabled_NoHandler_FatalTerminates` |

record.notes: §9.1.13.1 (cite.py OK) lets the implementor continue or terminate after a fatal I-O status; §14.6.13.1.3 5) (cite.py OK) terminates after a declarative when checking is enabled. Probes /tmp/adj/doc/doc-w1-s4/probe/p103a-d: checking off, no FILE STATUS use/no USE (85, 2023) -> OPEN '35' and READ '47' continue, NOT AT END ignored, exit 0; checking off + USE AFTER STANDARD ERROR (85, 2002, 2023) -> declarative runs, continues, exit 0; >>TURN EC-I-O CHECKING ON, no USE -> 'abnormal run-unit termination: EC-I-O-PERMANENT-ERROR (fatal): I-O status 35', exit 1; ON + USE -> declarative runs then terminates, exit 1. PARTIAL because the checking-off continue arm and the declarative-then-terminate arm are pinned by no test (only the checking-on no-handler arm is), and a host IOException in a sequential READ/WRITE escapes without a '30' (kb/Work PB1512, open, claims DOC-A.1-103). Side finding: the doc comment on FileStatus.LineRecordInvalidChar (FileStatus.cs:102-104) says a program without FILE STATUS or USE 'terminates here', which is false with checking off (default); comment should be corrected under PB1512 or a sweep.

row: | DOC-A.1-104 | **I-O status — the value placed when more than one value applies**, §9.1.13.1, required — A.1 says the internal procedure need not be documented, and it is documented here anyway so that a program can rely on the value it tests | **Exactly one I-O status value is placed per execution of an input-output statement, and the choice is fixed, never timing-dependent.** (1) **An unsuccessful value always wins over a successful one**: a successful-completion warning ('0x') never displaces a status that begins with another digit (`FileRegistry.NoRewindPhraseEffect` tests the first digit). (2) **Among unsuccessful values, the statement's preconditions are tested in the order its general rules state them, and the first one that fails supplies the status**: for a sequential READ, the open mode ('47') first, then a preceding unsuccessful READ or START ('46'), then the first READ of an absent OPTIONAL file ('10'), then a record locked by another file connector ('51'), and only then the physical retrieval (`FileConnector.SequentialReadGuard`). So a failing READ keeps its '47', '46' or '10' rather than reporting a '51' for a record it would never have read. (3) **Between two successful values, a value the statement's own general rules assign wins over a value only described in §9.1.13.2**: an `OPEN INPUT … WITH NO REWIND` of an OPTIONAL file that is not present reports **'07'** (§14.9.27.4 GR11), not '05' (§9.1.13.2 item 4 a)). The first READ of that file still reports the at-end '10', so the information '05' would have carried is not lost. Same in every edition. | `conformance:2023/pb317_open_no_rewind` |

record.notes: §9.1.13.1 (cite.py OK) 'If more than one value applies, the implementor determines which of the applicable values to place'; A.1-104 is required but need not be documented, so the row is VOLUNTARY (like 90/92/123/144). row: | DOC-A.1-111 | **LEAP-SECOND directive — whether a value greater than 59 seconds may be reported, and the maximum**, §7.3.17.4 GR2 (with §14.9.1.4 GR11, §15.21, §15.99), required + documented | **NO — the seconds position never holds a value greater than 59, with `>>LEAP-SECOND ON` or OFF, so the maximum is 59.** Every reported time comes from the one run-unit clock (`RunUnit.Current.Clock`, a .NET `DateTimeOffset`, which cannot represent a leap second): `ACCEPT … FROM TIME` (`AcceptSource.Time`, seconds in positions 5–6 of HHMMSScc), `FUNCTION CURRENT-DATE` and `FUNCTION FORMATTED-CURRENT-DATE` (`CobolDate.CurrentDate`), and `FUNCTION WHEN-COMPILED`, whose stamp is the compile-time clock reading baked into the program (`ProgramEmitter`). `>>LEAP-SECOND ON` is recognized from COBOL-2002 on (`LeapSecondDirectiveProcessor`) and changes only the ARGUMENT side of the date and time functions, where a seconds value of 60 is accepted — see item 112, which also records that SECONDS-PAST-MIDNIGHT never returns 86,400 or more. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-114 | **Line delimiter — specification of**, §12.4.5.10.3 GR2 (with §9.1.13.2 item 5, the '06' status), required + documented | **Written: CR LF (X"0D0A"), on every host operating system.** Every line a WRITE produces on a LINE SEQUENTIAL file is terminated by the two characters carriage return U+000D and line feed U+000A (`SequentialConnector.OpenWriter`), whether the program runs on Windows, Linux or macOS. A file written with plain WRITE statements holds each record followed by CR LF; when a WRITE has an ADVANCING phrase, that phrase decides where the delimiter falls relative to the record (§14.9.51.4 GR25). **Read: CR LF, a lone LF, or a lone CR each end a line**, and the last line of a file needs no delimiter at all: end-of-file ends it (`SequentialConnector.ReadPhysicalLine`). So files written on either Windows or Unix hosts are read line for line. An empty line reads as a record of spaces. The delimiter is never part of the record. **The '06' status:** when a READ fills the record area before it meets a delimiter or end-of-file, the READ succeeds with I-O status **'06'**, the record holds the leftmost characters, and the next READ continues from the next character of the same line (§14.9.30.4 GR15 NOTE 3). Example: the line `AAAAAAAA` read into `PIC X(5)` gives `AAAAA` with '06', then `AAA` padded with spaces and '00'. CR and LF are outside the line sequential character set (item 115), which is why a record area that contains one cannot be written. COBOL-2023 only: ORGANIZATION LINE SEQUENTIAL is a COBOL-2023 feature, and earlier editions reject it with COBOLNET0900. | `conformance:2023/pb964_ls_plain_write_after_after` |

row: | DOC-A.1-117 | **Listings — whether and when produced by the compiler, and the effect of logical conversion**, §7.3.18.3 GR1 + §6.5 (Clause 7), required + documented | **The compiler NEVER produces a source listing**, in any edition and under any option: the `cobol` command has no listing option, and a compilation writes only the assembly, its runtime configuration and the generated C# source (`<name>.g.cs`), which is not a listing of the COBOL source. Diagnostics go to standard error and identify the source line and column. Because there is no listing, **`>>LISTING` (ON, OFF, or with no operand) and `>>PAGE` are accepted and have no effect** (§7.3.18.3 GR1; §7.3.19): they are syntax-checked and hold no state (`DirectiveStateRegistry`, NONE HELD), and they compile from COBOL-2002 on. Like every `>>` directive they are rejected at COBOL-85 with COBOLNET0900. **Logical conversion (§6.5) has no effect on a listing**, because no listing exists. | `conformance:2002/pb725_directive_facility` |

row: | DOC-A.1-118 | **Locale specification — how the user default and system default locales are defined**, §8.2.1, required — A.1 says this need not be documented, and it is documented here anyway because the environment variables are the user's only control over the defaults | Both defaults are decided **once per run unit, when the run unit starts** (`LocaleState`, created with the `RunUnit`), and they are always two separate settings. **User default locale:** the environment variable **`COBOL_USER_LOCALE`** if it is set; otherwise the process's current .NET culture (`CultureInfo.CurrentCulture`, which on Unix follows `LANG`/`LC_ALL`); otherwise the root locale. **System default locale:** the environment variable **`COBOL_SYSTEM_LOCALE`** if it is set; otherwise the host's installed UI culture (`CultureInfo.InstalledUICulture`); otherwise the root locale. The variables' values are locale names in the item-119 notation, trimmed; `C`, `POSIX`, `root` or `INVARIANT` names the root locale. **At least one user default and one system default always exist**: in an environment with no locale data at all (.NET invariant globalization), both fall back to the root locale and the run unit starts normally. The current locale starts as the user default for every category (§14.6.6). A program can change the user default for the rest of the run unit with `SET LOCALE USER-DEFAULT TO …`, but it cannot change the system default (§8.2.1: the capability is not provided), so `LocaleState.SystemDefault` has no setter. Example: with `COBOL_USER_LOCALE=de-DE` and `COBOL_SYSTEM_LOCALE=fr-FR`, `FUNCTION LOCALE-DATE("20260924")` gives `24.09.2026` after `SET LOCALE LC_ALL TO USER-DEFAULT` and `24/09/2026` after `SET LOCALE LC_ALL TO SYSTEM-DEFAULT`. COBOL-2002 onward. | — |

record.notes: §8.2.1 (cite.py OK 'The implementor shall specify the manner in which the user default locale is defined'; OK 'The capability of setting the system default locale from COBOL is not provided'). row: | DOC-A.1-119 | **Locale specification — manner of implementation**, §8.2.1, required — A.1 says this need not be documented, and it is documented here anyway because it decides which locale names a program may use | **A locale is named by a BCP 47 / CLDR language tag**, and POSIX-style spellings are accepted and normalized: `es_ES.UTF-8` is `es-ES`, `de-DE@phonebook` is `de-DE` with the phonebook collation, and `C`, `POSIX`, `root`, `INVARIANT` and the empty name are the **root locale** (`LocaleIdentification.Normalize`). **A locale is available** when COBOL.NET has CLDR collation data for it, a site tailoring names it, or .NET recognizes it as a culture (`LocaleIdentification.IsAvailable`). A name that is none of these, such as `xx-NOWHERE`, is not available (EC-LOCALE-MISSING when a program selects it with checking on). The run unit keeps a current locale for **each of the six categories**, LC_COLLATE, LC_CTYPE, LC_MESSAGES, LC_MONETARY, LC_NUMERIC and LC_TIME, each set independently by SET LOCALE (`LocaleState`). **LC_COLLATE never comes from the host**: it is COBOL.NET's own collation table generated from Unicode CLDR release 48-2 / UCA 17.0.0 data, so a locale orders text the same way on every host. **LC_CTYPE, LC_MONETARY and LC_TIME** content comes from the nearest predefined .NET culture: the tag, then its parents (`sr-Latn-RS`, then `sr-Latn`, then `sr`) (`LocaleFacts`). When no ancestor is a .NET culture, or the process runs in .NET invariant-globalization mode, that content is incomplete: the invariant culture's values stand in, and an operation that needs the category sets EC-LOCALE-INVALID when checking is on. The implementor default when the environment supplies none is the root locale (item 118). COBOL-2002 onward. | `unit:LocaleStateTests.ExternalIdentification_IsNormalized_PerDeterminationL1`; `unit:LocaleStateTests.Availability_IsTheOneKnownLocaleRule`; `unit:LocaleStateTests.Set_SwitchesOnlyTheNamedCategories_AndTheyPersist` |

row: | DOC-A.1-120 | **Locale switch — whether a switch of the current locale by a non-COBOL runtime module is recognized by COBOL**, §8.2.1, conditionally required (documented if provided) | **No, for every category.** COBOL.NET never activates a non-COBOL module (a CALL cannot reach one, item 19). The only non-COBOL code that can share a run unit's process is a .NET host that activates a COBOL program, together with anything that host runs. The run unit reads the process culture **once, when it starts**, to determine its user and system default locales (item 118). After that, every locale-dependent operation uses only the run unit's own per-category state (`LocaleState`), and only SET LOCALE changes it. A later change of `CultureInfo.CurrentCulture`, `CultureInfo.DefaultThreadCurrentCulture` or the process's `LANG` by non-COBOL code is not utilized for LC_COLLATE, LC_CTYPE, LC_MESSAGES, LC_MONETARY, LC_NUMERIC or LC_TIME. Operations that are not locale-dependent never consult the process culture: DISPLAY of a floating-point or numeric item, NUMVAL and UPPER-CASE give the same result under `LANG=de_DE.UTF-8` or `tr_TR.UTF-8` as under `LANG=C`. A host that wants a different locale sets `COBOL_USER_LOCALE` (or its culture) before the run unit starts. COBOL-2002 onward. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-122 | **National literals — number of hexadecimal digits that map to a national character**, §8.3.3.5.3 SR5, required + documented | **FOUR.** Each group of four hexadecimal digits in an `NX"…"` (or `NX'…'`) literal is one national character: the UTF-16 code unit with that value, which is also one national character position. `NX"004100420043"` is the three characters `ABC`, `FUNCTION LENGTH(NX"00410042")` is 2, and `FUNCTION ORD(NX"00E9")` is 234 (é is U+00E9). A character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane is written as its two surrogate code units and occupies two positions: `LENGTH(NX"D83DDE00")` is 2. A literal whose digit count is not a multiple of four, such as `NX"414"` or `NX"004100"`, is rejected with **COBOLNET1635** (`CobolLiteral.HexGroupViolation`). NX literals exist from COBOL-2002 on; at COBOL-85 they are COBOLNET0900. The check is not yet made for an NX argument of an intrinsic function written without the FUNCTION keyword (kb/Work PB1393). | `conformance:2023/r03_hexadecimal_national_and_boolean_literals` |

record.notes: §8.3.3.5.3 SR5 (cite.py OK §8.3.3.5.3 5)) leaves the digits-per-national-character count to the implementor; COBOL.NET's is 4 (determination D-N1, one UTF-16 code unit). Probes /tmp/adj/doc/doc-w1-s4/probe/p122.cob at --std 2002 and 2023: VALUE NX"004100420043" -> ABC; LENGTH(NX"00410042") -> 0002; LENGTH(NX"D83DDE00") -> 0002; ORD(NX"00E9") -> 234; --std 85 -> COBOLNET0900. p122b.cob: NX"414" and NX"004100" -> COBOLNET1635. row: | DOC-A.1-125 | **NULL — the value of NULL**, §8.4.3.7.4 GR1 (object references) + §8.4.3.10.4 GR1–GR3 (data, program and function addresses), required — A.1 says this need not be documented, and it is documented here anyway because a pointer's NULL is visible in its storage image | **Object reference:** NULL is the .NET null reference, which never refers to an object, so `O = NULL` is true exactly when O refers to no object. **Data-pointer, program-pointer and function-pointer:** NULL is the default value of each pointer type (`ManagedPointer.Null`, `ProgramPointer.Null`, a `FunctionPointer` with no name), and it is distinct from every address `SET … TO ADDRESS OF` can produce: no data item, program or function has that address. **Storage image:** a NULL pointer of every category is eight X"00" bytes, the zero address, as in GnuCOBOL, IBM and Micro Focus. Any real address has a nonzero image (item 216). Every pointer and object-reference item starts as NULL, and SET … TO NULL restores it. The message-tag NULL (GR4) does not arise, because USAGE MESSAGE-TAG belongs to the message control system, which is not provided (COBOLNET1943). COBOL-2002 onward. | `conformance:2002/pb557_pointer_class_initial_value_is_null`; `unit:PointerImageTests.Null_OfEveryCategory_IsTheZeroAddress`; `conformance:2023/pb452_function_address_runtime` |

row: | DOC-A.1-126 | **OBJECT-COMPUTER paragraph — the default object computer**, §12.3.6.4 GR3 and GR4, required + documented | **The default object computer is the .NET runtime the program is compiled for**: the `Microsoft.NETCore.App` 10.0 shared framework (`net10.0`, named in the `.runtimeconfig.json` written beside every compiled assembly), on whatever operating system and processor it runs. There is only ONE object computer, so the default is the same whether the paragraph is written without computer-name-1 (GR3), omitted altogether with no containing source unit supplying one (GR4), or written with any computer-name (item 127: the name is accepted and identifies nothing). A program therefore behaves identically in all three cases: the same native collating sequence and character classification, and the PROGRAM COLLATING SEQUENCE and CHARACTER CLASSIFICATION clauses have the same effect with or without a name. Same in every edition. At COBOL-85 an OBJECT-COMPUTER paragraph that carries a clause must also carry computer-name-1; a paragraph with no clauses may omit the name in every edition. | `conformance:2023/pb373_object_computer_name_inert` |
